#Step 1

set.seed(123)

n <- nrow(data)
train_index <- sample(1:n, size = 0.7 * n)
train_data <- data[train_index, ]
test_data  <- data[-train_index, ]

y_var <- "W" 


model <- lm(formula = W ~ OPS + ERA + FIP + HR_Bat + Rdrs, data = train_data)

summary(model)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = W ~ OPS + ERA + FIP + HR_Bat + Rdrs, data = train_data)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -8.8739 -2.7112  0.3021  2.7023  7.7840 
## 
## Coefficients:
##              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  -9.71790   15.53797  -0.625   0.5342    
## OPS         234.29701   23.58345   9.935 5.79e-14 ***
## ERA         -13.60010    1.99841  -6.805 7.25e-09 ***
## FIP          -3.03004    2.63106  -1.152   0.2544    
## HR_Bat       -0.04970    0.02582  -1.924   0.0594 .  
## Rdrs          0.08094    0.06171   1.312   0.1950    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 4.033 on 56 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.919,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.9118 
## F-statistic: 127.1 on 5 and 56 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
y_var <- "W" 

numeric_cols <- names(train_data)[sapply(train_data, is.numeric)]
numeric_cols <- numeric_cols[-1]                  # drop first column
numeric_cols <- setdiff(numeric_cols, y_var)     # drop response variable

correlations <- train_data %>%
  select(all_of(numeric_cols)) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), 
                   ~ cor(.x, train_data[[y_var]], use = "complete.obs"))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Correlation") %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(Correlation)))
correlations

#Step 2

plot(train_data$DH, train_data$y_var)

train_data$DH_centered <- train_data$DH - mean(train_data$DH)
train_data$DH_c2 <- train_data$DH_c^2
model1 <- lm(
  W ~ OPS + ERA + FIP + HR_Bat + Rdrs + DH_centered + DH_c2,
  data = train_data
)
summary(model1)

vif(model1)

plot(model1, which = 1)

plot(model1, which = 2)

hist(residuals(model), 
     main = "Histogram of Residuals for Model 1",
     xlab = "Residuals")

plot(model, which = 1)

plot(model, which = 2)

hist(residuals(model), 
     main = "Histogram of Residuals for Model 1",
     xlab = "Residuals")

#install.packages("lmtest")
library(lmtest)
dwtest(model)
## 
##  Durbin-Watson test
## 
## data:  model
## DW = 1.7267, p-value = 0.1447
## alternative hypothesis: true autocorrelation is greater than 0

The curvature slightly improved the model. The p-value for the polynomia is less than 0.05 indicating statistical significance. The assumptions remained relatively the same, looking at constant variance, nomality, and indepedence. The vifs are relatively the same also, the polynomial model is slightly higher which is expected with more predictors. R^2 adjusted is slightly higher in the model with the curvature which leads me to the conclusion that the polynomial model is a slight improvement over the first model.

#step3

#model1 <- lm(W ~ OPS + ERA + FIP + HR_Bat + Rdrs + DH_centered + DH_c2, data = train_data)

model2 <- lm(W ~ OPS*HR_Bat + OPS + HR_Bat + ERA + FIP + Rdrs + DH_centered + DH_c2, data = train_data)
summary(model2)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = W ~ OPS * HR_Bat + OPS + HR_Bat + ERA + FIP + Rdrs + 
##     DH_centered + DH_c2, data = train_data)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -8.5055 -2.8505  0.3392  2.3795  7.4653 
## 
## Coefficients:
##              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) -29.64669   44.97486  -0.659  0.51263    
## OPS         253.09451   63.08099   4.012  0.00019 ***
## HR_Bat        0.08265    0.21664   0.382  0.70433    
## ERA         -13.15635    1.99266  -6.602 1.97e-08 ***
## FIP          -2.65803    2.61099  -1.018  0.31329    
## Rdrs          0.06259    0.06539   0.957  0.34284    
## DH_centered   0.09955    0.64679   0.154  0.87826    
## DH_c2        -0.47912    0.25440  -1.883  0.06515 .  
## OPS:HR_Bat   -0.15210    0.28997  -0.525  0.60209    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 3.93 on 53 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.9272, Adjusted R-squared:  0.9162 
## F-statistic: 84.38 on 8 and 53 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
vif(model2)
## there are higher-order terms (interactions) in this model
## consider setting type = 'predictor'; see ?vif
##         OPS      HR_Bat         ERA         FIP        Rdrs DH_centered 
##   21.523785  201.386456    4.924234    4.824031    1.273746    3.495266 
##       DH_c2  OPS:HR_Bat 
##    2.051104  303.835408

The interaction term is not statistically significant. The p value is greater than 0.05 indicating that there is no evidence that the interaction between hr bats and ops is statistically significant. It also has a lower adjusted r-squared value than the reduced model meaning that the second model is being punished for including the interaction term. In theory, the interaction between OPS and HR_bats does increase interpretability. In the context of baseball, OPS or on base percentage + slugging percentage does matter for teams that also hit more home runs.

The current model, No there is not need for variable screening. If we were to expand the model though to all possible second terms yes there would be too many variables and there would be a lot of multicollinearity.

library(MASS)

boxcox(model1)

Since the model shows a lamda of around 1 for most of the 95% confidence interval there is no need of a transformation of the y variable.

#OPS + ERA + HR_Bat + Rdrs + DH_centered + DH_c2
plot(train_data$OPS, train_data$y_var, main = "OPS vs Wins", ylab = "OPS", xlab = "Wins")

plot(train_data$ERA, train_data$y_var, main = "ERA vs Wins", ylab = "ERA", xlab = "Wins")

plot(train_data$HR_Bat, train_data$y_var, main = "HR_Bats vs Wins", ylab = "HR_Bats", xlab = "Wins")

plot(train_data$Rdrs, train_data$y_var, main = "Rdrs vs Wins", ylab = "Rdrs", xlab = "Wins")

plot(model1$residuals ~ train_data$OPS)

plot(model1$residuals ~ train_data$ERA)

plot(model1$residuals ~ train_data$HR_Bat)

plot(model1$residuals ~ train_data$Rdrs)

plot(model1$residuals ~ train_data$DH_centered)

plot(model1$residuals ~ train_data$DH_c2)

Y does not require a box-cox transformation. None of the residuals don’t require a transformation fulfill constant variance. The DH_c2 might seem alarming but that is without the centering variable which shows constant variance. None of the predictor variables based off of any of the plots or residual diagnostics seem to require a transformation. Everything seems normal so there is no need for a transformation of Y or any of the predictor variables.

#Step 7

DH_mean <- mean(train_data$DH)

test_data$DH_centered <- test_data$DH - DH_mean
test_data$DH_c2 <- test_data$DH_centered^2


pred_test <- predict(refined_model, newdata = test_data)


RMSE <- sqrt(mean((test_data$Y = pred_test)^2))
RMSE

## [1] 83.64077
mean_W <- mean(train_data$W)
mean_W
## [1] 79.51613
sd_W <- sd(train_data$W)   
sd_W
## [1] 13.57764

Compared to the week 8 model, it slightly outperforms. The r adjusted value is higher for the refined model. But from what I can tell, the model is not accurate. For context the mean is 79.5 wins and the standard deviation is 13.58 wins. The RMSE is greatly larger than the standard deviation.
